cards.title: 3.5.1 Horticulture: meaning and importance
body: **Horticulture** is the branch of agriculture that produces and handles **fruits, vegetables, flowers, ornamental plants, spices and herbs**, and also cares for gardens and green spaces. Compared with field crops it is **intensive**: small areas, high value, more water, labour and care per hectare, and the crops are often first raised in a **nursery**.
**Why it matters:**
- **Nutrition:** fruits and vegetables are rich in **vitamins and minerals** (tomato, kale, carrot, orange, papaya, guava).
- **Industry:** flowers for perfume; fruit and vegetables for canning (tomato paste), juice and jam.
- **Medicine:** many herbs are used in modern and traditional medicine.
- **Commerce:** fresh produce and cut flowers earn **foreign exchange**.
- **Beauty (aesthetic value):** street trees and gardens in Asmara, parks and homes.
- **Social value:** parks and gardens are places to meet; markets such as the Asmara vegetable market bring sellers and buyers together.

cards.title: Branches of horticulture
head: Branch
Deals with
Examples
rows: Banana, citrus, mango, guava, papaya, grape
Tomato, onion, cabbage, kale, pepper, potato, lettuce
Design and care of gardens, parks, roadsides

cards.title: Memory hooks
body: **Pomo-** = apple/fruit (pomme). **Oler-** = pot herb/vegetable. **Flori-** = flower. "**P**ick fruit, **O**lives in the pot, **F**lowers on the table."

cards.title: 3.5.2 Production systems in horticulture
body: - **Open-field production:** crops grown outside in natural soil and climate (most vegetables around Keren, Asmara and along the Anseba).

- **Protected production:** in **glasshouses (greenhouses), poly-tunnels** or under **plastic covers**. In a greenhouse temperature, light and humidity are **controlled**; in low tunnels and cloches they are only **partly regulated**. Used for high-value crops such as tomatoes, peppers and cut flowers.
- **Hydroponics:** plants grown **without soil**, with all nutrients supplied **in a solution** (lettuce, onion, tomato).
By scale, horticulture ranges from a few square metres in **home gardens** (best near towns, where the family can water and sell) to thousands of hectares on large farms.

cards.title: 3.5.3 Nurseries and site selection
body: A **nursery** is a place where seedlings are raised with water, shade and protection, then moved to the field. Types:
- **Peasant nursery:** rural farmers raise their own seedlings.
- **Standard nursery:** produces seedlings on a **commercial** scale (e.g. Ministry of Agriculture forestry and fruit nurseries).
- **Intermediate (temporary) nursery:** keeps mature seedlings from a standard nursery for a short time until they are distributed.
By how plants are grown, nurseries are also **field nurseries** (in beds) or **container nurseries** (pots, poly-tubes).
**Site selection:** suitable **climate** and protection from **wind**; **level** land; clean **water** free of salts; **fertile** soil; easy **road access**. Fence it from goats.
**Steps to set up:** clear the site → level → lay out paths, beds and structures (shade, water tank, store) → prepare seedbeds and soil mix.

cards.title: Seedbeds and soil mixes
body: **Tools:** hoes, spades or shovels, pickaxes, rakes, string and pegs.
- **Raised beds:** **15–20 cm above** ground. Used where **drainage** is needed (wet areas, heavy soils, rainy season).
- **Sunken beds:** **10–15 cm below** ground. Used to **conserve moisture** in dry, low-rainfall places; water is supplied by irrigation.

**Soil mix:** plain field soil is either too **clayey** (tight, badly drained) or too **sandy** (holds little water). In a shallow pot or box the base stays wet because there is no soil below to draw water down, so use a **coarser, lighter mix** that drains and still holds moisture: for example **soil + sand + compost** (change the ratio to suit your soil: add more sand to a clay soil), or sand + compost, or well-decomposed manure.

cards.title: 3.5.5 Routine nursery practices
body: 1. **Sowing and mulching:** vegetables and annuals are sown in seedbeds, seed boxes or **plug trays** and later transplanted; tree seed is sown directly into containers or densely in beds and then pricked out. Cover the bed with grass **mulch** to help germination and stop weeds; **remove** it as soon as seedlings emerge.
2. **Transplanting (pricking out):** water the bed first, lift seedlings with soil on the roots, hold them by the leaves, not the stem.

3. **Shading:** young seedlings need shade (the "growth shade period"); reduce shade gradually before field planting (**hardening**). Straw is cheap and local; plastic netting gives even shade but costs more.
4. **Weeding:** competition is severe in containers. Hand-weed while weeds are young; good **sanitation** is the cheapest control.
5. **Thinning:** remove extra seedlings so the rest have enough space, light, water and nutrients.
6. **Root and shoot pruning:** cut roots growing out of the container; balance the shoot to the root. Fruit trees get **formative pruning** (training) from the nursery stage.

7. **Watering and protection:** water newly sown beds often; use a can with a **fine rose** so seeds are not washed out. Water less often in cool seasons and heavy soils; once or twice a day in hot weather. Watch for **damping-off** (seedlings collapse at soil level).
8. **Grading:** discard weak, poor seedlings; about **10–20 %** culls is normal.

cards.title: The nursery routine in order
body: **"Some Men Take Shade When The Proper Water Gets Hot"**: Sow, Mulch, Transplant, Shade, Weed, Thin, Prune, Water, Grade, Harden.

cards.title: 3.5.6 Vegetative propagation: budding and grafting
body: **Vegetative propagation** uses roots, stems or leaves instead of seed. Methods: **cuttings, layering, division, budding and grafting**. The new plant is a **clone**: identical to the mother, so a good mango or orange variety stays true.

A grafted fruit tree has two parts: the **rootstock (stock)**, which forms the root system (hardy, disease resistant, grown from seed, cuttings, suckers or layers), and the **scion**, the upper part that carries the **desired variety** (fruit quality).
- **Grafting** joins a scion with **two or more buds** to a stock; used for new plants and to **top-work** (change the variety of) old trees, e.g. peach, mango.
- **Budding** uses a scion of **a single bud** on a piece of bark; quick and easy, and the most common way to propagate **citrus**. Chip and shield (T) budding are the main tropical methods.
**Key rule:** the **cambium** (the green growing layer between bark and wood) of stock and scion must touch. Both form **callus** cells that interlock and heal the union.

steps.text: Make a **vertical cut 3–4 cm** long through the bark of the stock, just to the wood.
Make a **horizontal cut 1–2 cm** across the top of it (a T; across the bottom for an inverted T).
Cut the bud **shield**: start about 1 cm below the bud and finish a little above it, taking a thin sliver of wood.
Open the bark flaps with the back of the knife and **push the shield in** until it is fully enclosed.
**Wrap** firmly with budding tape, leaving the bud exposed. Remove the tape once the bud has taken.

cards.title: Grafting methods and tools
body: - **Whip (tongue) graft:** small stems **6–12 mm** thick, stock and scion of equal size. The scion is 5–15 cm long with 2–3 buds. Make matching **diagonal cuts of 3.5–5 cm**, then a **reverse "tongue" cut** a third of the way down each, half as long, so they interlock. Match the cambium on at least one side and wrap with tape.

- **Side-veneer graft:** potted plants 6–12 mm thick; a 5–7 cm cut into the side of the stock with a notch at its base; the scion is cut to fit, inserted and wrapped. Cut back the stock once the scion grows.
- **Bark** and **cleft grafts:** on **large stems**, for **top-working** an old tree to a new variety. **Wedge grafting** is a cleft graft on small stems.

**Tools and materials:** **secateurs** (collect and trim wood), a sharp single-bladed **budding/grafting knife**, a **saw** (top-working), mallet and wedge for cleft grafts, **grafting wax** to seal cuts against drying and infection, **polyethylene tape**, cloth tape or rubber strips, labels, plastic or paper bags to protect scions, short nails for bark grafts.

cards.title: 3.5.7 Propagation by cuttings
body: A **cutting** is a piece of stem (sometimes root) that forms roots and becomes a new plant. Tools: cutting wood, secateurs, soil mix, pots. Easy plants: **lantana, grape, coleus**, rose, sugarcane setts, cassava. Cuttings are also used to raise clonal **rootstocks**.

- **Softwood cuttings:** young soft shoots **10–15 cm** long; remove the leaves from the lower third; dip in **rooting hormone**; insert in a well-drained, **sterile** medium; keep under **intermittent mist** until rooted; then **harden off** by misting less or moving to shade in pots for some weeks.
- **Semi-hardwood cuttings:** from the **matured part of this season’s growth**; prepared the same way; misting less often.

- **Hardwood cuttings:** dormant wood **6–20 mm** thick cut into **15–30 cm** pieces, the base cut **just below a node**; hormone; bundles stored **upside down** in moist sterile peat (callusing box) until a yellowish-white **callus** forms at the base; plant out before many roots form, burying all but the top bud.

cards.title: 3.5.8 Propagation by layering
body: **Layering** makes roots form on a stem **while it is still attached to the mother plant**, which keeps feeding it. It suits plants that are hard to root by other methods, but gives only a **few** plants.

- **Air layering** (hard stems, branches 1–2 cm thick): remove a **ring of bark 1–3 cm** wide, **15–30 cm** from the branch tip; apply hormone; wrap in a ball of **moist moss or compost** and cover with **polythene** or foil; when roots show, cut below the wrap and pot it. Mango, rubber plant, croton, camellia.
- **Simple layering:** bend a low branch to the ground and **bury** part of it, leaving the tip out; wounding and hormone help. Climbing rose, jasmine, oleander.
- **Serpentine (compound) layering:** a long flexible branch is pegged down at **several places**, giving several plants.
- **Trench layering:** the whole branch is laid in a trench and nicked in several places; many shoots root along it (willow).
- **Mound layering (stooling):** cut the plant back near the ground, heap soil over the new shoots, keep moist; when rooted, separate them. Apple rootstocks, croton, peach.

cards.title: Layering stays on the mother until rooted. A cutting must survive on its own stores.
3.5.9 Propagation by division; hardening and transport
body: **Division** cuts a clump or underground storage organ into pieces, each with enough **stems, leaves, roots and buds** to survive transplanting. Used for plants with many stems or **offshoots**, **bulbs** (garlic, onion sets, narcissus), **corms** and **cormels**, **rhizomes** (canna, ginger), **tubers** (potato) and **suckers/offshoots** (**banana, date palm**, ferns, orchids, daylilies).

**Hardening** prepares nursery seedlings for the shock of field planting: growth slows, food storage increases and tissues toughen, so hardened plants root faster and resist drought and temperature extremes. Start well **before** transplanting:
- expose plants to cooler than optimum temperatures (cool areas) or warmer than optimum (hot areas);
- **reduce watering gradually**, without letting the seedlings wilt;
- move shaded seedlings into **full sun** step by step.
**Transport:** container seedlings travel more easily than bare-root field seedlings; protect them from damage, wind and sun, especially on long trips.

cards.title: 3.5.10 Site selection for a horticultural farm
body: Fruit trees are **perennial**: once an orchard is planted it cannot easily be moved, so assess the site fully first. Vegetables also need the right environment and market to be profitable.

- **Climate:** each crop has its temperature, rainfall and light needs (citrus and mango in warm lowlands and the escarpment; apple, potato and cabbage in the cool highlands); plant **windbreaks** where needed.
- **Terrain:** suitable altitude and slope.
- **Soil and drainage:** the right soil type and drainage for the crop.
- **Irrigation water:** essential in arid and semi-arid Eritrea.
- **Economics:** check that the crop will be **profitable** (market distance, prices) before planting.

cards.title: 3.5.11 Garden layout and land preparation
body: Draw a **plan** of the garden to record planting and harvest dates and the area of each crop. Mark out beds from the plan.
- Beds **1.0–1.2 m wide**, so all work (weeding, harvesting) can be done from the path without stepping on the bed; length as convenient.
- Example: plots **6 m wide**, separated by **1 m grass paths**, each divided into beds **1.2 m** across with **60 cm** temporary paths.
- Put a **fence or hedge** around the garden against animals.
- **Succession planting:** a crop calendar so one crop follows another and the garden is always producing. **Companion planting:** growing crops that suit each other together.
- Commercial layout depends on the farm scale, crop, variety, equipment, season and technology.

cards.title: Garden plan
body: Dividing the garden into three plots makes rotation easy: e.g. leafy vegetables → fruit vegetables (tomato, pepper) → root crops and legumes.

cards.title: Worked example — how many beds fit in a plot?
cards.problem: A plot is 6 m wide. Beds are 1.2 m wide with 60 cm paths between them. How many beds fit, and how much width is used?

steps.text: Try 4 beds: 4 × 1.2 m = 4.8 m of beds, plus 3 paths × 0.6 m = 1.8 m. Total 6.6 m: too wide.
Try 3 beds: 3 × 1.2 m = 3.6 m, plus 2 paths × 0.6 m = 1.2 m. Total **4.8 m**.
So **3 beds** fit, leaving 1.2 m: either a fourth narrower bed or wider edge paths.

cards.title: Preparing a home or school garden
body: **First preparation:**
1. Wet the area (especially hard dry clay) and let it dry partly for two days.
2. Loosen the soil to about **30 cm** with a spading fork; remove weeds.
3. Water gently and rest one day; wait longer if there are big clods (sun, cool nights and water break them).
4. Clay soil: mix in **not more than 2.5 cm** of sand (more lets soluble fertiliser wash through too fast).
5. Add **8 cm** of compost or aged manure to poor (very sandy or very clayey) soils, **2.5 cm** to good soils; mix into the top 30 cm.
6. Dig twice if the soil is heavy; water and rest a day.
7. Level and shape the beds; add fertilisers and pH correctors: **lime** for acid soil; for alkaline soil, sulphur or acid-forming fertilisers such as ammonium sulphate.
8. Plant or transplant.
**Replanting:** dig after removing old crops, shape beds, water, add about 2.5 cm of compost and fertiliser, plant.

cards.title: Double digging and pit preparation
body: **Double digging** (home and school gardens, medium and clay soils, every 3–4 years):
1. Dig a trench **28–30 cm deep** and **56–70 cm wide** across the bed; carry that topsoil to the far end.
2. Loosen the subsoil in the trench a further **15–30 cm**; spread manure or compost on it.
3. Dig the topsoil of the next strip onto the manured subsoil of the first; loosen and manure the second strip’s subsoil.
4. Repeat to the end; fill the last trench with the soil from the first.
Result: the bed is loosened **45–60 cm** deep and needs no double digging for **2–4 years**.

**Pits for trees:** usually **60 × 60 × 60 cm**; **100 × 100 × 100 cm** in soil with a hardpan. Keep topsoil and subsoil apart, mix topsoil with manure to refill, plant at the nursery depth, water and **mulch**. For close-planted orchards dig a **furrow** along the row instead.

cards.title: 3.5.12 Sowing, transplanting and field care
body: Most horticultural crops are sown in a nursery and **transplanted**; **cucurbits** (pumpkin, watermelon, cucumber) are usually sown directly.
- **Adapted varieties:** use varieties recommended for your area; do not use unknown seed for commercial growing, even if it is free.
- **Germination test** before sowing: seed deteriorates fast in hot humid conditions, even in an opened can.
- **Depth:** small seeds **0.6–1.2 cm** deep; too deep and they cannot emerge or they rot.

- **Transplant** only healthy, vigorous, **stocky** seedlings with **4–6 true leaves**; this takes about **3–6 weeks** in warm climates (fastest: tomato, cabbage, broccoli, lettuce; slowest: pepper, eggplant). Tomato: 15–20 cm tall with a pencil-thick stem; cabbage: 6-leaf stage; eggplant: 10–12 cm. Old, overgrown seedlings suffer more transplant shock. Transplant in the **afternoon** or on cloudy days, with soil on the roots.
- **Thinning** gives remaining plants room. **Mulching** with straw, banana leaves or plastic cuts evaporation and runoff, keeps soil temperature and moisture even, and suppresses weeds.
- **Tree pruning** builds a strong framework, keeps trees healthy and of manageable size: formative pruning, removal of dead and diseased wood, size control, and stimulation of new fruiting wood.
- **Watering:** the right amount at every stage; too little or too much lowers yield.
- **Fertiliser:** manure, compost or mineral fertiliser by broadcasting, base-dressing, band placement, top-dressing, liquid or **foliar** feeding.

cards.title: 3.5.13 Post-harvest handling
body: **Post-harvest handling** covers every operation from harvest to the consumer that affects quality and storage life. In developing countries up to **50 %** of fresh produce can be lost: of 100 kg of tomatoes harvested, 50 kg may never be eaten, because of bruising in transport and poor handling at markets.
- **Highly perishable:** tomato, strawberry, guava, leafy vegetables. **Less perishable:** onion, potato, pumpkin.
- Handle each crop to suit it: potatoes and onions can go in **sacks**; tomatoes need **boxes or crates**.

- The chain: harvest at the right stage in the **cool** part of the day → **clean** → **sort** (remove damaged, diseased and green potato tubers) → **grade** by size → **pack** → transport quickly in shade → sell or store cool. NARI’s seed potato work shows sorting, grading into boxes and packing in jute sacks.

questions.q: Complete the photosynthesis equation that your unit uses to explain how a cereal crop such as sorghum builds its food: $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_} \xrightarrow{\text{\_\_\_\_\_\_}} \text{Sugar} + \text{\_\_\_\_\_\_}$$ Fill in the three blanks in order, and name the pigment written above the arrow.
questions.answer: Blank 1 = Light Energy; Blank 2 = Chlorophyll; Blank 3 = O2, i.e. $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$. The pigment above the arrow is chlorophyll.
why: **Recall the unit equation.** The unit defines photosynthesis as the biological process in which light energy is transformed into chemical energy, and writes it as $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.
**Fill the first blank (energy input).** The only input still missing from the left-hand side is the energy source, so the first blank is Light Energy (sunlight).

**Fill the second blank (the substance above the arrow).** The unit places Chlorophyll above the reaction arrow. Chlorophyll is the green pigment of the leaf (the leaf is the site of photosynthesis) that captures the light energy needed to drive the reaction.
**Fill the third blank (by-product).** The right-hand side already shows Sugar; the second product released by the plant is oxygen gas, so the third blank is O2.

**Conclude.** Blank 1 = Light Energy, Blank 2 = Chlorophyll, Blank 3 = O2, giving the complete equation $$\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Light Energy} \xrightarrow{\text{Chlorophyll}} \text{Sugar} + \text{O}_2$$.

questions.q: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands sows two plots on the same day: Plot A with field peas and Plot B with common beans. Several days later the farmer notices that in Plot B the cotyledons have been pushed above the soil surface, while in Plot A the cotyledons are still below the soil. (a) Name the type of germination shown in Plot A and in Plot B. (b) Explain which elongating structure is responsible in each case. (c) In which plot, if any, do the cotyledons act as the first photosynthetic leaves?
questions.answer: (a) Plot A (peas) = hypogeal germination; Plot B (common beans) = epigeal germination. (b) Hypogeal: the epicotyl elongates while the cotyledons stay below the soil. Epigeal: the hypocotyl elongates and pulls the cotyledons above the soil. (c) Only in Plot B (epigeal), where the cotyledons act as the first photosynthetic leaves.
why: **Recall the two germination types.** The unit defines two types based on cotyledon movement: hypogeal germination, in which the cotyledons remain below the soil surface while the epicotyl elongates (peas, broad beans), and epigeal germination, in which the hypocotyl elongates and pulls the cotyledons above the soil surface (common beans, castor oil).
**Classify Plot A (field peas).** In Plot A the cotyledons stay below the soil; peas are named in the unit as an example of hypogeal germination.
**Classify Plot B (common beans).** In Plot B the cotyledons are carried above the surface; common beans are the unit's example of epigeal germination.
**Name the elongating structures.** Plot A (hypogeal): the epicotyl elongates and the cotyledons remain underground. Plot B (epigeal): the hypocotyl elongates, lifting the cotyledons out of the soil.

**Decide where cotyledons photosynthesise.** Only in Plot B, because the unit states that in epigeal germination the cotyledons are pulled above the soil surface where they act as the first photosynthetic leaves.

**Match castor oil.** The unit lists castor oil under epigeal germination, so the hypocotyl elongates and the cotyledons are carried above the soil.

questions.q: Explain why the seed of a crop such as maize can germinate to a strong seedling only when three environmental conditions are present. Name the three conditions given in the unit and state the specific role of each one.
questions.answer: The three conditions are adequate water (softens the seed coat and activates the enzymes), oxygen (needed for aerobic respiration) and optimum temperature (generally $$10^\circ\text{C}$$ to $$35^\circ\text{C}$$, with about $$20^\circ\text{C}$$ optimum for most crops). Without all three, the embryo cannot resume growth and germination fails or is weak.
why: **State what germination is.** The unit defines germination as the process by which a seed embryo wakes from dormancy and begins to grow into a seedling.
**Name the three environmental conditions.** Successful germination requires adequate water, oxygen and an optimum temperature.

**Give the role of each condition.** Water softens the seed coat and activates enzymes; oxygen supports aerobic respiration; temperature must be in the range of about $$10^\circ\text{C}$$ to $$35^\circ\text{C}$$ with $$20^\circ\text{C}$$ being optimum for most crops.
**Conclude.** All three conditions must be met together, which is why waterlogged or very cold soil gives poor emergence even when good seed is sown.

questions.q: A wheat crop near Keren shows a pale yellowish-green colour. An extension agent observes that the symptom is visible on the old, lower leaves while the young upper leaves are still green, and explains that this happens because nitrogen is highly mobile in the plant. According to the unit, why does a nitrogen shortage affect the old, lower leaves before the young leaves?

options.A: Because nitrogen is immobile in the plant, so it stays fixed inside the leaves that first received it
options.B: Because the plant moves nitrogen out of the old leaves to support new growth, and those old leaves are the first to run short
options.C: Because old leaves have the smallest leaf area, so they lose nutrients to the soil before the young leaves do
options.D: Because old leaves receive the least sunlight, so their chlorophyll breaks down before that of the upper leaves

why: **Recall the unit's Pro-Tip.** The unit's Pro-Tip states that nitrogen is highly mobile in plants and that when a deficiency occurs the plant moves nitrogen from old leaves to support new growth.

**Link mobility to the visible pattern.** Because nitrogen can be withdrawn from the old, lower leaves and redirected to the growing points, the older leaves are the first to fall short of nitrogen and therefore the first to show the pale yellowish-green deficiency colour.
**Check option A.** A contradicts the unit: nitrogen is described as highly mobile, not immobile, so A is false.

**Check option C.** Nutrient shortage is caused by internal redistribution to new growth, not by old leaves having a smaller area or by loss of nutrients to the soil; no such process is given in the unit, so C is false.
**Check option D.** The unit gives no role for sunlight differences among leaves in nitrogen deficiency; the symptom is explained by nutrient mobility, not by a light gradient, so D is false.
**Conclude.** Only option B states the unit's reason: nitrogen is moved out of the old leaves to support new growth, so the old leaves yellow first.

**Check option A.** A reverses the definition: micronutrients (trace elements) are required in tiny amounts, not in large quantities, so A is false.
**Check option B.** The unit states that carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are obtained from air and water, so they are not applied as fertilizer; B is false.
**Check option D.** The unit classifies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium as primary nutrients and calcium, magnesium and sulphur as secondary nutrients, which is the reverse of D, so D is false.

**Confirm option C.** C correctly combines the figure of $$16$$ essential elements with the unit's list of micronutrients (Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl) and their tiny but equally essential requirement, so C is the only correct statement.

questions.q: A sorghum field of $$1$$ hectare near Keren has a plant population of $$30{,}000$$ plants. On average, each plant carries $$3$$ heads (panicles), and each head contains $$168$$ grains. Calculate the total number of grains produced in the hectare and express your answer in scientific notation. Then state, in one sentence, what this figure represents for the farmer.
questions.answer: Total grains = $$30{,}000 \times 3 \times 168 = 15{,}120{,}000$$ grains per hectare = $$1.512 \times 10^{7}$$ grains. This is the hectare's total grain (potential seed) harvest from the sorghum crop.
why: **Name the quantities given.** Plant population = $$30{,}000$$ plants/ha; heads per plant = $$3$$; grains per head = $$168$$; area = $$1$$ ha. The unit classifies sorghum as a cereal grown for its edible starchy seeds, so the harvestable unit is the grain.

**Choose the working formula.** Total grains = plant population x heads per plant x grains per head, i.e. the seed output is built up from the number of seed-bearing plants and the seeds carried by each head.
**Calculate the grains per plant.** $$3 \times 168 = 504$$ grains per plant.
**Multiply by the plant population.** $$30{,}000 \times 504 = 15{,}120{,}000$$ grains per hectare.
**Convert to scientific notation.** Place one digit before the decimal point: $$15{,}120{,}000 = 1.512 \times 10^{7}$$ grains.

**Interpret the result.** The figure is the total number of grains (potential seeds) the hectare can yield; because it is a cereal, these grains are the starchy food harvest the farmer sells or stores, and the same figure is the largest possible number of seeds available for sowing the next season.

questions.q: A sesame field of $$1$$ hectare in the lowlands of Eritrea carries $$40{,}000$$ plants. Each plant bears on average $$3$$ capsules, and each capsule contains $$50$$ seeds. Find the total number of seeds produced per hectare and write it in scientific notation.
why: **List the data.** Plants per hectare = $$40{,}000$$; capsules per plant = $$3$$; seeds per capsule = $$50$$. The unit lists sesame as an oil crop, so its harvested propagules are the seeds.
**State the formula.** Total seeds = plant population x capsules per plant x seeds per capsule.
**Substitute and multiply step by step.** $$3 \times 50 = 150$$ seeds per plant; $$40{,}000 \times 150 = 6{,}000{,}000$$ seeds per hectare.
**Convert to scientific notation.** $$6{,}000{,}000 = 6 \times 10^{6}$$ seeds per hectare.

questions.q: A field pea plot of $$1$$ hectare on a farm near Mendefera has $$250{,}000$$ plants. Each plant forms $$4$$ pods, and each pod contains $$5$$ seeds. (a) Calculate the total number of seeds per hectare. (b) If the farmer must keep $$20\%$$ of these seeds for sowing next season, how many seeds are kept for sowing?
why: **List the data.** Plants per hectare = $$250{,}000$$; pods per plant = $$4$$; seeds per pod = $$5$$; sowing reserve = $$20\%$$. Field peas are listed in the unit as a pulse grown for protein-rich seeds.
**Formula for total seed number.** Total seeds = plant population x pods per plant x seeds per pod.
**Compute part (a).** $$4 \times 5 = 20$$ seeds per plant; $$250{,}000 \times 20 = 5{,}000{,}000$$ seeds per hectare.
**Compute part (b).** Sowing reserve = $$\frac{20}{100} \times 5{,}000{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000$$ seeds, which can also be written $$1 \times 10^{6}$$ seeds.
**Interpret.** The farmer harvests 5 million seeds and must set aside 1 million of them as the seed stock for the next planting, leaving 4 million seeds as the food/grain share.

questions.q: An agricultural extension officer working with farmers in the Eritrean highlands and western lowlands is preparing a planting plan based on the agronomic classification of field crops given in the unit. The crops under consideration are: teff, niger seed (nihug), faba bean, cotton, sorghum, sesame and sugarcane. (a) Sort all seven crops into their correct agronomic groups (cereals, pulses, industrial crops, forage crops). (b) Name the sub-groups of the industrial crops into which niger seed, cotton and sugarcane fall. (c) The officer advises a farmer who grew sorghum this season to rotate it next season with faba bean rather than with another cereal. Using the unit's description of pulses, justify this advice with one biological reason. (d) Which of the seven crops is a native of the Abyssinian center of diversity, and what does teff's origin there tell us about the crop?
questions.answer: (a) Cereals: teff and sorghum. Pulses: faba bean. Industrial crops: niger seed (oil), sesame (oil), cotton (fiber) and sugarcane (sugar). Forage crops: none of the seven crops listed. (b) Niger seed and sesame = oil crops; cotton = fiber crop; sugarcane = sugar crop. (c) Pulses such as faba bean are leguminous plants able to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, so a faba bean crop restores the nitrogen that the sorghum cereal removed, improving soil fertility for the next crop. (d) Teff is native to the Abyssinian center of diversity (Eritrean Highlands); because its wild progenitor Eragrostis pilosa is native there, teff was domesticated locally thousands of years ago.
why: **Recall the four agronomic groups.** The unit classifies field crops as cereals (grown for edible starchy seeds, rich in carbohydrates), pulses (leguminous plants grown for protein-rich seeds and valued for fixing atmospheric nitrogen), industrial crops (raw materials for industries), and forage crops (grown as livestock feed, preserved as hay or silage or grazed).
**Assign the cereals.** Teff (Eragrostis tef) and sorghum are stated in the unit to be cereals because they are grown for their edible starchy seeds; the unit's cereal examples include both.
**Assign the pulse.** Faba bean (Vicia faba) is listed in the unit's crop table as a pulse (legume), so it forms the single pulse entry among the seven crops.

**Assign the industrial crops and their sub-groups.** Niger seed (nihug) and sesame are oil crops, cotton is a fiber crop and sugarcane is a sugar crop, so all four are industrial crops. The unit's sub-groups are oil crops (sesame, linseed), sugar crops (sugarcane, sugar beet) and fiber crops (cotton, sisal).

**Check for forage crops.** None of the seven crops is described in the unit as a forage crop: forage crops are grown specifically as livestock feed and conserved as hay or silage. The forage group therefore has no member in this list, which is an important negative finding for the officer's plan.

**Justify the rotation advice (part c).** The unit states that pulses are leguminous plants valued for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil. Sorghum, as a cereal, takes nutrients out of the soil during the season, whereas a faba bean crop adds nitrogen to the soil. Rotating sorghum with faba bean therefore restores soil nitrogen and improves the fertility of the field for the following cereal crop.

**Identify the Abyssinian native and interpret it (part d).** The unit's table gives teff's native center of diversity as the Abyssinian Center (Eritrean Highlands); niger seed, barley, emmer wheat, linseed, safflower, chickpea, lentil and sesame are also named as crops domesticated there. The unit's Did You Know note adds that the wild progenitor of cultivated teff, Eragrostis pilosa, is native to this center, which confirms that teff was domesticated locally thousands of years ago.

**Conclude the classification.** Cereals: teff, sorghum. Pulse: faba bean. Industrial crops (oil): niger seed, sesame; (fiber): cotton; (sugar): sugarcane. Forage: none of the seven. Rotation with faba bean is justified because pulses fix atmospheric nitrogen, and teff belongs to the Abyssinian center of diversity, confirming local domestication.

questions.q: A farmer in the Eritrean highlands plans a four-field rotation and can choose from barley, linseed, chickpea and sisal. (a) Classify each crop into its agronomic group and, for any industrial crop, name its sub-group. (b) Which two of these crops would you recommend the farmer grow in order to add nitrogen to the soil, and why? (c) State one reason from the unit why a crop such as sisal is described as a fiber crop rather than a cereal.
questions.answer: (a) Barley = cereal; linseed = industrial crop, oil crop; chickpea = pulse; sisal = industrial crop, fiber crop. (b) Chickpea would be recommended, because it is a leguminous pulse valued for fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil; linseed is an oil crop and does not add nitrogen. (c) Sisal is grown as a raw material for industry (its fiber), whereas cereals are grown for their edible starchy seeds, so the two crops belong to different agronomic groups.
why: **Recall the classification criteria.** Cereals are grown for edible starchy seeds rich in carbohydrates; pulses are legumes grown for protein-rich seeds and for nitrogen fixation; industrial crops are raw materials for industries, including oil crops (sesame, linseed) and fiber crops (cotton, sisal).
**Classify each of the four crops.** Barley is named in the unit as a cereal; linseed appears in the unit's oil crop examples; chickpea is named among pulses; sisal is listed as a fiber crop.

**Answer part (b).** Only chickpea is a leguminous pulse able to fix atmospheric nitrogen, so it is the crop that adds nitrogen to the soil; linseed, barley and sisal do not have this property in the unit.

**Answer part (c).** Sisal is a fiber crop because it is grown as an industrial raw material, while a cereal is grown for its edible starchy seed; the harvested product and the purpose of growing it are therefore completely different.

questions.q: Three Eritrean buyers place orders with a farming cooperative: an oil press needs raw material, a flour mill needs starchy grain, and a textile factory needs natural fiber. From the crops teff, niger seed, sesame, chickpea, cotton and sugarcane, (a) select one crop for each buyer and name the agronomic group it belongs to; (b) state which of the six crops are pulses and explain the soil benefit they provide; (c) name the industrial sub-group of any remaining crop that is an industrial crop but was not chosen in (a).
questions.answer: (a) Oil press: niger seed or sesame (oil crops within the industrial crops group). Flour mill: teff (cereal). Textile factory: cotton (fiber crop within the industrial crops group). (b) Chickpea is the only pulse among the six; as a leguminous plant it fixes atmospheric nitrogen in the soil and so improves soil fertility. (c) The remaining industrial crop is sugarcane, which is a sugar crop.
why: **Match each buyer to a crop group.** The unit's industrial crops include oil crops (sesame, linseed), fiber crops (cotton, sisal) and sugar crops (sugarcane, sugar beet); cereals are grown for edible starchy seeds. An oil press needs an oil crop, a flour mill needs a cereal, and a textile factory needs a fiber crop.
**Answer part (a).** Oil press: niger seed or sesame. Flour mill: teff, because teff is a cereal with starchy grain. Textile factory: cotton, because cotton is a fiber crop.

**Answer part (b).** Chickpea is the only pulse listed; the unit states that pulses are leguminous plants grown for protein-rich seeds and valued for their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen in the soil, which raises soil fertility for the next crop.
**Answer part (c).** Sugarcane was not selected by any of the three buyers and is an industrial crop of the sugar crop sub-group.
**Check that no crop is left unclassified.** Teff = cereal; niger seed and sesame = oil crops; cotton = fiber crop; sugarcane = sugar crop; chickpea = pulse. All six crops are accounted for.

questions.q: Give four harmful effects and two benefits of weeds.
questions.answer: Harmful: compete for nutrients, water, light and space (yield loss); harbour insects and diseases; reduce quality; health problems; water contamination; lower land value. Benefits: animal feed, compost/manure, medicine, oil, thatch, soil and water conservation.
why: Step 1: Competition and pests.
Step 2: Uses as feed and materials.
questions.tip: Weeds are plants in the wrong place.

similar.q: How do you recognise a sedge?
similar.a: Grass-like leaves with a solid triangular stem.

questions.label: 3.3 Practice — cultural practices

questions.q: Why is inter-row cultivation done at about knee height in sorghum and maize?
questions.answer: To kill weeds growing in the open spaces before the canopy closes; it also loosens the crust so rain infiltrates, conserves moisture, aerates the soil and promotes nitrification.
why: Step 1: Weeds compete most early.
Step 2: Later the crop shades them out and cultivation would cut roots.
questions.tip: Weed while you still can walk between rows.

similar.q: Name three crops in which inter-row cultivation is done.
similar.a: Maize, sorghum, pearl and finger millet.

questions.label: 3.3 Practice — cultural practices

questions.q: How can a farmer tell that a cereal is ready for harvest, and what happens if harvest is late?
questions.answer: Plants turn yellow or brown and the grain is hard when bitten. Late harvest causes shattering, bird and rodent losses and lodging.
why: Step 1: Colour change.
Step 2: Bite test.
Step 3: Too late → losses.

similar.q: Distinguish traditional and modern harvesting.
similar.a: Traditional: sickle and oxen trampling. Modern: combine harvester cuts, threshes and cleans at once.

questions.label: 3.3 Practice — cultural practices

questions.q: List five features of a good seed store.
questions.answer: One door, no windows (openings covered by wire mesh); smooth crack-free floor; sealed against insects and rodents; cool, dry and ventilated; clean; walls sprayed about once a year; first in, first out; labels and records.
why: Step 1: Keep pests out.
Step 2: Keep it dry and cool.
Step 3: Manage stock.

similar.q: What does "first in, first out" mean?
similar.a: Seed that entered first leaves first.

questions.label: 3.3 Practice — cultural practices

questions.q: Explain three negative effects of mono-cropping.
questions.answer: Soil fertility falls (same nutrients removed each year); diseases and insects of that crop build up; its typical weeds (e.g. Striga in sorghum) multiply; so yields decline.
why: Step 1: Nutrient depletion.
Step 2: Pest/disease build-up.
Step 3: Weed build-up.
questions.tip: Same crop, same problems, every year.

similar.q: Give a highland example of mono-cropping.
similar.a: Wheat or barley on the same field every year.

similar.a: Seeds of two crops mixed and broadcast together.

questions.label: 3.4 Practice — cropping systems

questions.q: List four advantages of inter-cropping.
questions.answer: Yield advantage; yield stability (insurance); diverse products; more income; labour spread; soil and water conservation; N from the pulse for the cereal.
why: Step 1: More total yield and less risk.
Step 2: Better use and protection of soil.
questions.tip: Two baskets are safer than one.

similar.q: Why mix more than two crops in dry areas?
similar.a: To spread risk: some crop survives a drought.

questions.label: 3.4 Practice — cropping systems

questions.q: Sole maize yields 3 t/ha and sole bean 1 t/ha. An intercrop gives 2.4 t maize and 0.5 t bean. Find the LER and say what it means.
questions.answer: LER = 2.4/3 + 0.5/1 = 0.8 + 0.5 = 1.3; the intercrop gives 30 % more than sole crops on the same land.
why: Step 1: Partial LERs: 0.8 and 0.5.
Step 2: Sum = 1.3 > 1.

similar.q: What does LER = 0.9 mean?
similar.a: The intercrop is less productive than sole crops.

questions.label: 3.4 Practice — cropping systems

questions.q: In alley cropping, shading of the crop is prevented by

options.B: pruning the hedgerows before and during cropping
options.C: planting the crop under the trees

why: Step 1: Hedges are cut back so light reaches the crop.
Step 2: Prunings become mulch/green manure.

similar.q: Why use leguminous trees in alley cropping?
similar.a: They add nitrogen to the soil.

similar.q: Why are fallow periods short in Eritrea today?
similar.a: There is not enough land for the growing population.

questions.q: Plan a three-year rotation for a lowland field and give two reasons for the order.
questions.answer: E.g. sorghum → cowpea or groundnut → sesame (then sorghum again). The legume adds N for the next crop; changing crop families breaks pest, disease and Striga cycles.
why: Step 1: Start with a cereal.
Step 2: Follow with a legume.
Step 3: Add a different family (oil crop).

questions.q: List five criteria for selecting a nursery site.
questions.answer: Suitable climate and shelter from wind; level land; clean water free of salts; fertile soil; easy road access (and a fence against animals).
why: Step 1: Weather and wind.
Step 2: Land and soil.
Step 3: Water and access.

similar.q: What is the first step in preparing a nursery site?
similar.a: Site clearing, then levelling and layout.

questions.q: Describe the damage weeds cause in a nursery and the cheapest way to control them.
questions.answer: They compete strongly for nutrients and water in small containers (and for light if left uncontrolled), and harbour pests; good sanitation is the cheapest control, with hand weeding of young weeds.
why: Step 1: Small soil volume → severe competition.

similar.q: Why is grading done in a nursery?
similar.a: To discard poor seedlings that would die or yield poorly; 10–20 % culls is normal.

questions.answer: Softwood: young soft shoots 10–15 cm, leaves removed from the lower third, kept under mist. Hardwood: dormant wood 6–20 mm thick, 15–30 cm long, callused in moist peat (upside down) before planting.

questions.q: Give three hardening practices for nursery seedlings.
questions.answer: Expose them to below-optimum temperatures (cool areas) or above-optimum (hot areas); reduce water gradually without wilting; move shaded seedlings gradually into full sun.
why: Step 1: Temperature.
Step 2: Water.
Step 3: Light.
questions.tip: Toughen with temperature, water and sun.

similar.q: Why harden seedlings?
similar.a: So they survive transplant shock, root faster and resist drought.

questions.answer: Climate (temperature, rain, light, wind); terrain (altitude, slope); soil and drainage; availability of irrigation water; economics (profit, market).
why: Step 1: Physical factors.

similar.a: Greater transplant shock; roots are damaged more.

questions.answer: Reduces evaporation and runoff; keeps soil temperature and moisture even; suppresses weeds (organic mulch also adds organic matter).

questions.answer: Bad handling (bruising, heat, delay, wrong packing) causes losses up to 50 % and poor quality; good handling (harvest in cool hours, clean, sort, grade, pack in crates, quick shaded transport) keeps produce fresh and saleable.
